result:
I've always loved maps that are wrong.

Not wrong in a frustrating way — not the kind that sends you down a dead-end road at midnight — but wrong in an honest, hopeful way. Old maps with sea monsters curling in the empty parts of the ocean. Subway maps that pretend a tangled city is just a few clean, colored lines. The treasure map a kid draws on notebook paper, where the kitchen is an island, the couch is a mountain range, and X is buried, very seriously, under the dog.

Every map is a confession. It says: *This is too big to hold all at once, so here's the part I thought mattered.*

We all carry those kinds of maps inside us, too, and they're all gloriously inaccurate.

I have a map of my childhood street that is about three houses long and impossibly wide. In real life it was probably an ordinary street. In memory, the hill was steep enough to be dangerous on a bike and gentle enough to be worth it, and the house at the corner had a garden that felt like a jungle you could get lost in on purpose. It wouldn't help anyone navigate. That was never its job.

We carry maps of people, too. The version of a friend as they were when they were seventeen and invincible and terrible at returning phone calls. The version of a parent as they were when they seemed to know how everything in the house worked — the fuse box, the car engine, the exact right soup for a bad day. Those maps get outdated. People redraw themselves. If we're lucky, we let them hand us a new draft.

And we carry maps of ourselves that are hilariously out of scale. The embarrassing thing we said three years ago takes up an entire continent. The kind thing we did without thinking barely gets a dot. The future is always drawn in the corner with a lot of blank space and maybe a hopeful little arrow: *Here Be Something.*

I like the blank spaces best.

Cartographers used to fill them in with monsters because empty paper felt unbearable. We do the same thing, just with worries or daydreams. We invent a whole storm system over next week’s conversation. We invent gold over next year. Most of the time what we actually find there is much smaller and much better than either: a Tuesday afternoon that goes unexpectedly well, a song on the radio we’d forgotten we loved, someone laughing in a kitchen.

Maybe a good map isn’t one that gets everything right. Maybe it’s one that gets you close enough to start wandering, and curious enough to keep going when the road looks nothing like the drawing.

So I’m trying to hold my maps a little looser these days. Pencil instead of ink. Big margins for notes. Room in the corners for a monster or two, just in case — not because I believe in them, but because I like a world that admits it isn’t finished being discovered.

After all, the best places I’ve ever found weren’t marked X at all. They were just off the edge of what I thought I knew, waiting for me to misread the map in exactly the right direction.
